hints: Start with the job description in the stem: telomerase adds nucleotides to telomeres, so ask yourself what happens to telomeres each time normal DNA is replicated without enough of this enzyme.
Remember the rule: more telomerase means telomeres stay long and divisions can continue, less telomerase means telomeres get shorter until the cell must stop dividing.
walkthrough:
**Recall what telomeres do**

Think of telomeres as protective caps on the ends of chromosomes. Every time DNA replicates, a little bit of the end is lost, so the caps get shorter and shorter.

Telomerase rebuilds them by adding nucleotides back on.

**Link telomerase level to number of divisions**

High telomerase keeps telomeres long, so the cell can keep dividing many times. This is what we see in stem cells and cancer cells.

Low telomerase lets telomeres shorten, so after a certain number of divisions the cell cannot divide safely any more.

**Apply this to normal body cells**

Most normal body (somatic) cells have very low telomerase activity. That is why they have a limited lifespan for division, often called the Hayflick limit, which helps protect against uncontrolled growth.

options.A: High telomerase protects genes by rebuilding telomeres, it does not damage genes during replication.
options.B: High telomerase in cancer cells does the opposite, it allows unlimited division and so promotes, not limits, tumour growth.
options.C: Stem cells need high, not low, telomerase to divide an unlimited number of times and keep replacing tissues.
options.D: Correct, low telomerase in normal body cells means telomeres shorten with each division, so these cells can only divide a limited number of times.
